fixes.explanation: Infants, friend. Paul says he couldn't address them as spiritual, but as worldly, “…as infants in Christ.” I think that's a kind way to say there's growing left to do. And he still opens by calling them “Brothers.”

Elders would mean grown and seasoned, and Paul says the opposite. He calls them infants in Christ. Then he says he gave them milk, not solid food, because they weren't ready (1 Corinthians 3:2). Nobody starts out with the solid stuff.

Not strangers, friend. Paul calls them “Brothers” and says they are infants “in Christ.” He doesn't call them strangers anywhere in these verses. The picture is of babies who still have growing to do.
Paul doesn't call them lazy. The word is jealousy, and it comes with dissension. He says that's why they are still worldly.
Mere men. Paul asks, “are you not mere men?” That's his response to hearing “I follow Paul…” and “I follow Apollos…” I think he's pulling them back down to earth so they can look up again.

Servants. Paul says Apollos and himself are “…servants through whom you believed…” and that the Lord has assigned to each his role. The role came from the Lord. That's a pretty good reason not to brag about it.
Not quite. Paul says they are servants through whom the Corinthians believed. He says the Lord has assigned to each his role. The text doesn't call them leaders the church chose.
Close, but flip it. Paul says, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.” So Apollos watered, and God is the one who made it grow. The answer is False.
Followers were the whole argument in Corinth, but they aren't the measure here. Paul says each will be rewarded according to his own labor. The reward follows the work, not a headcount.
Flock isn't the word here. Paul has been talking about planting and watering, so he says, “you are God’s field, God’s building.” Stay with the farm, friend.

No army in this verse. Paul keeps to the garden and says, “you are God’s field, God’s building.” After all that talk of planting and watering, it fits. The field is where God makes things grow (1 Corinthians 3:7).

No flood in this passage. Paul says the Day will bring each work to light and, “It will be revealed with fire…” Then “the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work.” Fire is the test here, friend, not water.
Paul doesn't call it hidden. He says, “…for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.” Holy is the word he uses. He also says God's Spirit dwells in them (1 Corinthians 3:16).

True, and it sounds backwards on purpose. Paul says, “…he should become a fool, so that he may become wise.” He's speaking to anyone who thinks he is wise in this age. I think that's a call to let go of that kind of wisdom first.
